episode_thesis: Greg Jensen argues the investing world is being reshaped by three things: a shift from 1980s free-market policy to modern mercantilism, an AI capex boom that is still early (the bubble is ahead, not behind), and record capital concentration in US assets. In his view mercantilism and military spending are inflationary (base case US inflation around 3%), fiscal limits are now binding in developed countries so bonds diversify less, and the right response is to survive across many scenarios through global diversification rather than pick winners. He pairs this with Bridgewater's process of compounding written, machine-readable knowledge, a separate AI investor, rare overrides of the system and radical transparency.

worldview_premises.premise: The economy is moving from the 1980s regime of small government and free markets to modern mercantilism (tariffs, state control, trade as zero-sum, independence from other countries), a reaction to China's rise and the hollowing of the Western middle class; investors must adapt rather than assume the old economy.
worldview_premises.support: historical regime analogy and political observation

worldview_premises.premise: Collapse of US goodwill abroad drives populist, mercantilist politics, first populist right and then populist left if policies fail, with less international cooperation. International institutions have lost their function and US domestic institutions are fading.
worldview_premises.support: polling on support for the US (2024 to 2025), election observations (AfD, Reform, France); source not named

worldview_premises.premise: Capital concentration in US assets (equity and illiquid) is a risk factor. The US is shifting from an exceptional place to invest to a normal one with a higher risk premium, though this is muted at index level by the AI offset.
worldview_premises.support: US equities' worst relative performance versus the world in common currency in 15 years while headline averages look calm

worldview_premises.premise: Index averages hide stress. Look underneath them (S&P ex-AI names, gold) to see shifts the headline averages miss.

Mercantilism is inflationary: tariffs and resilient supply chains replace cheapest sourcing, reversing 30 years of productivity gains, and military spending creates demand for labour and goods with no supply into the real economy.
worldview_premises.support: reasoning with examples (India tariffs above China's, Germany's and Europe's defence build-up)

worldview_premises.premise: AI investment gives growth with low labour intensity and so a weak labour market and initially disinflationary effect. It follows a J-curve, so the strongly disinflationary phase is further out.
worldview_premises.support: US growth of about 2-2.5% would be about 1% without AI

worldview_premises.premise: Populist control of the central bank that lowers real rates into an AI boom would be inflationary.

Fiscal limits depend on domestic savings, productivity and willingness to hold the currency (Japan at 300% of GDP versus Brazil at 60-80%). Developed economies such as the UK, and increasingly the US, are constrained, and beyond the limit fiscal expansion weakens the currency and equities and raises rates.
worldview_premises.support: Brazil, UK and Germany comparisons; Bridgewater's own measures

worldview_premises.premise: Bonds are no longer the 30-year diversifier because fiscal limits shift correlations, and fiscal policy responds to disinflation, so bonds hedge deflation less well. They still deserve a place after the rise in real yields.

Fiscal supply and AI ecosystem spending (tech firms turning from net savers to spenders, private credit) create a shortage of capital, pushing real rates up against US central bank pressure to lower them.
worldview_premises.support: reasoning on capital supply and demand

worldview_premises.premise: AI capex is driven by strategic, non-profit motives of firms whose businesses are threatened (and by beliefs about enormous power), so spending continues beyond normal return discipline. The current phase is a resource grab for power, chips and scientists, which is dangerous but not yet a bubble.
worldview_premises.support: observed behaviour of Musk, Altman, Google; Abu Dhabi data-center anecdote

worldview_premises.premise: AI-generated efficiency gains will make current chips and data-center assets depreciate fast.
worldview_premises.support: reasoning from labs' goals and Google's protein-folding result

worldview_premises.premise: Vendor financing is Nvidia building a controlled ecosystem against Google's full stack, using scarce chips as leverage, not bubble-style demand creation. Fewer than about a thousand frontier scientists make talent the binding constraint, and poaching slows progress.
worldview_premises.support: competitive-position argument and his network (numbers are his estimate)

worldview_premises.premise: The way to compound wealth is to avoid really bad outcomes. After 15 years of US-equity success, a US-only portfolio is a trap and diversification has been abandoned at the wrong time.
worldview_premises.support: compounding logic; Bridgewater's survival record since 1991

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are a probabilistic game: you must be wrong often and right more, and handle incomplete information and mistakes. Machines surpassing humans in poker is an analogy for edge when machines learn faster than humans.

Knowledge compounds only if beliefs are written down, stress-tested and encoded in human- and machine-readable form with a record of changes. AI works best when processes are redesigned around it (Amazon robots) rather than copying human tasks.
worldview_premises.support: Bridgewater's expert-system history and the Amazon analogy

decision_process.practice: Write down beliefs, stress-test them, and translate them into algorithms (expert system). Research counts only when translated into compounded knowledge (plain-English reasoning plus code); otherwise no credit.
decision_process.why: knowledge must compound and be auditable

decision_process.practice: Build portfolios to survive a wide range of possible worlds rather than pick the best asset, with much broader global diversification than most investors hold, including Europe and China.
decision_process.why: avoiding bad outcomes is how compounding works; winners and losers are unknown

decision_process.practice: Rely on risk control as the main driver of survival, accepting that all are flawed.
decision_process.why: Bridgewater survived 1991 when competitors did not

decision_process.practice: Hold some bonds again after the rise in real yields, but treat them as riskier and a weaker diversifier than before.
Look beneath headline index averages (S&P ex-AI, gold) for shifts.

Run an AI agent investor as a separate entity designed around AI, to generate independent ideas uncorrelated with Pure Alpha, and now merge it back. Machines learn rules rather than copy human intuition.
decision_process.why: avoid copying human flaws; security and technology reasons

decision_process.practice: Overrule the system rarely and with discipline, and speed new research into positions before it is fully systematised. Give researchers independence.
decision_process.why: overruling barely helps on average; COVID lesson

decision_process.practice: Radical transparency with feedback aimed up at leaders; measure whether managers draw out criticism. Hire for a balance of open-mindedness and assertiveness; shift from CIO-centralised decisions to independent investors.
decision_process.why: lets the best ideas win; failure modes are not speaking up and not listening

decision_process.practice: Reflect on pain rather than run from it (Dalio's 'pain plus reflection equals progress'); Dalio's succession took 15 years.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Conflict of interest context: Jensen was in the first round of OpenAI investors and wrote the first check into Anthropic (personally), yet argues AI is not overhyped and the bubble is ahead.
The bubble-ahead claim and the 'more dangerous but not a bubble' phase have no measured valuation, capex or return thresholds, so they cannot be falsified or timed.

Tension on AI and inflation: AI's low labour intensity is called disinflationary now (C07-4, growth about 1 pt of 2-2.5%), but the J-curve claim says the strongly disinflationary phase is further out and the first phase only absorbs resources.
Breakeven inflation number is garbled in the caption ('around 2 and a2'); the ledger fix reads it as about 2.5%.

He expected mercantilism to push money out of the US and concedes it has had less effect than expected, but keeps the theme as one of three; the AI offset is offered as the explanation without quantification.
AI contribution to growth is quoted for different years (about 1 point this year, about 1.5 of 2.5 next year) from memory without source.
The AI agent investor is said to have produced alpha since 2024, with no figures or independent evidence.
Statements on the collapse of US goodwill ('biggest collapse we've ever seen') and fewer than a thousand frontier scientists are unsourced.
Known-imperfect historical analogues can be embedded in process (Spanish flu), which is a caveat on his own use of regime analogies such as the 1980s turn versus mercantilism.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs he names: relative performance of US equities versus the world and of S&P ex-AI names; gold; US inflation versus breakeven (about 2.5%) and Fed tolerance; fiscal deficits, domestic savings and currency and rate reaction to fiscal announcements (UK, US); real yields and the pace of AI-related and fiscal capital demand; defence spending; AI capex and power, chip and scientist scarcity; the Fed's voting split; US goodwill and populist electoral shifts. Horizon: the next one to two years for inflation and growth; longer for the AI bubble and diversification.
reader_inferences: (reader) The framework implies stress should show first in sub-components (US ex-AI equities, gold, UK gilts) before in headline indices, so tracking relative indicators is the observable test of his regime thesis.

(reader) His 'survive across worlds' rule and his three-theme view point to risk balancing across inflation, growth and fiscal-stress scenarios rather than a single forecast; the base case is stated but not the sizing.

(reader) The inflation call (3%) and the bond view (weak diversifier) are linked: if AI disinflation or a deflation shock arrives first, his own argument says bonds would hedge less well because fiscal policy responds.
